title: Public Endpoints vs Private Endpoints
description: Compare public and private endpoints to understand the security and networking trade-offs for Azure services.

data.text: By default, most Azure services expose a public endpoint accessible over the internet. Private endpoints add a private IP inside your VNet, giving you a second, secure path to the same service.

cards.title: Public Endpoint
cards.description: Default access over the internet with IP restrictions or firewalls.

cards.title: Private Endpoint
cards.description: Private IP inside your VNet with traffic over Azure backbone.

data.title: Hybrid Approach
data.text: You can use both public and private endpoints for the same service. For example, expose Key Vault privately to your VNet while allowing a third-party vendor to use the public endpoint with IP firewall rules.

data.title: Evaluate Access Methods
data.description: For each scenario, decide whether a public endpoint, private endpoint, or both is appropriate.
steps: A mobile app needs to call a Logic App from anywhere.
A production app in a VNet needs to read from Key Vault.
A partner vendor needs to upload files to your Storage account.
data.expectedOutcome: You can justify why each scenario uses public, private, or both endpoint types.

data.caption: A public endpoint resolves to a public IP over the internet; a private endpoint resolves to a private IP inside the VNet through a private DNS zone.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    APP["App in VNet"] --> DNS{"Which hostname\ndoes it resolve?"}
    DNS -->|public name| PUBIP["Public IP\nof the service"]
    PUBIP --> FW["Service firewall\nmust allow the client"]
    FW --> SVC["Azure service"]
    DNS -->|privatelink name| PRIVIP["Private IP\nin the delegated subnet"]
    PRIVIP --> PE["Private endpoint\nNIC"]
    PE --> SVC
    NET["Internet client"] --> PUBIP
    NET -.->|blocked when public\naccess is disabled| FW

data.text: Create a Private Endpoint with the CLI

A private endpoint is a network interface in your subnet that connects to a specific sub-resource of a service. Creating the endpoint is only half the job: you must also disable public access (if the service supports it) and make sure DNS resolves the service name to the private IP.

data.title: Private endpoint for a storage account
data.content: The `--group-id blob` selects the Blob sub-resource. The private DNS zone makes `mystorage12345.blob.core.windows.net` resolve to the private IP inside the VNet.
data.code:
# Turn off public network access
az storage account update \
  --name mystorage12345 \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --public-network-access Disabled

# Create the private endpoint in the app subnet
az network private-endpoint create \
  --name pe-storage-blob \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --vnet-name vnet-demo \
  --subnet snet-app \
  --private-connection-resource-id $(az storage account show \
      --name mystorage12345 \
      --resource-group rg-demo \
      --query id --output tsv) \
  --group-id blob \
  --connection-name conn-storage-blob \
  --private-dns-zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net

data.title: The DNS zone must be linked to every VNet that needs it
data.text: The most common private-endpoint failure is not networking — it is DNS. If the private DNS zone `privatelink.blob.core.windows.net` is not linked to the client VNet, the name keeps resolving to the public IP and traffic never reaches the private endpoint. Also remember that creating a private endpoint does not disable the public endpoint by itself; you must set public network access to Disabled or restrict it with firewall rules.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Public endpoints are simple but expose services to the internet.
Private endpoints remove public exposure and keep traffic on Azure backbone.
You can use both for the same service when needed.
data.takeaway: Default to private endpoints for any sensitive service accessed from a VNet.
